Neonatal koalas exhibit several distinctive morphological features that reflect their extreme altriciality at parturition. A newborn joey, having gestated for a period of 35 days [tg = 35 days] under a maternal body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], emerges at a remarkably undeveloped state. At this birth event, the neonate measures a mere 0.08 centimeters [Lb = 0.08 centimeters] in total body length, with the head being disproportionately long relative to the trunk during this early developmental window. This altricial neonate weighs approximately 0.5 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.5 grams], a diminutive mass that underscores the marsupial strategy of a short gestation followed by an extended period of postnatal development within the maternal pouch. The tiny size of the newborn is an adaptation to a limited gestational investment, allowing the mother to conserve resources while the joey undergoes most of its organogenesis and growth while permanently attached to a teat inside the pouch, where it will remain for many months.

Within the protected environment of the pouch, the suckling juvenile undergoes a dramatic transformation over its first year of life. The nursing offspring, entirely dependent on its mother's milk, experiences a rapid increase in both length and mass. Field records indicate that the time since birth at weaning is approximately 365 days [tx = approximately 365 days] when measured at a body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At this milestone of nutritional emancipation, the weaned juvenile typically attains a total body length of about 6 centimeters  and a wet weight of approximately 2000 grams [Wwx = approximately 2000 grams]. This dietary transition from milk to a diet consisting almost exclusively of eucalyptus leaves marks a critical juncture in the life history of the species. The weaned young must develop a specialized gut microbiome capable of detoxifying the phenolic compounds found in eucalypt foliage, a process that requires significant physiological adaptation and a period of adjustment following the cessation of lactation.

Sexual maturation in the koala is a gradual process that culminates at an age considerably later than that of weaning. A seminal study by Martin and Handasyde in 1999 documented that females typically attain puberty between 1.5 and 2 years of age, while males may not be able to hold territory until later, though they likely mature early. More precisely, the time since birth at puberty for reproductively viable organisms is generally accepted to be 547.5 days [tp = 547.5 days] when measured under a standard body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. At the onset of puberty, a young female koala will have reached a total body length of approximately 12.7 centimeters [Lp = approximately 12.7 centimeters] and a wet weight in the range of 6000 grams [Wwp = 6000 grams]. This body weight represents the achievement of a threshold where sufficient energy reserves can be directed toward the energetic demands of gestation and lactation, rather than solely toward continued somatic growth, marking the transition from a sub-adult into a breeding adult mammal.

The ultimate body size attained by a fully grown, reproductively active adult koala reflects the species' relatively low metabolic rate and its adaptation to a nutritionally poor diet. An adult in prime condition may reach a maximum recorded total body length of 13.5 centimeters [Li = 13.5 centimeters], a measurement that corresponds to the snout-to-vent length of a large, healthy individual. The ultimate wet weight for a mature koala in prime condition is approximately 8300 grams [Wwi = approximately 8300 grams], though this value can vary considerably depending on the quality of the local eucalyptus habitat. This asymptotic mass is achieved only after several years of growth and represents the culmination of the juvenile growth phase. During the breeding season, a sexually active adult male may maintain a high body condition to compete for access to females, while a gravid female must sustain the substantial metabolic cost of supporting a developing foetus and subsequently producing large quantities of energy-rich milk to provision the suckling juvenile in her pouch.

The reproductive physiology of the koala is finely tuned to the constraints of its folivorous diet, with a maximum rate of reproduction that is relatively low when compared to other marsupials of equivalent size. Under optimal temperature conditions typical of a healthy individual, maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is approximately one offspring per year [Ri = approximately one offspring per year]. This slow reproductive output is a direct consequence of the high energetic cost of lactation, which represents the bulk of maternal investment. The mean milk production for a lactating female is estimated at 47,298.63 joules per day  when measured at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a value derived from the combination of the daily reproduction rate and the adult body mass, reflecting the intense energetic drain on the mother. This substantial energy transfer to the single joey, combined with the specialized dietary requirements, likely contributes to the species' recorded lifespan, which for females can range from 13 to 18 years, with a calculated mean life span of 5475 days [am = 5475 days] under a standard body temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C].
